Nemzetközi egyezmények, európai uniós jogszabályok, kétoldalú államközi megállapodások és a nemzeti vízgazdálkodási előírások” – írták. Magyarázatuk szerint a Duna aktuális természetes vízhozamát úgynevezett zsinórüzemben vezetik tovább: ez azt jelenti, hogy a beérkező vízmennyiséget lényegében változatlanul bocsátják tovább az alvízi szakaszokra. Magyarországon pedig a Dunán nem is működik olyan vízlépcső, ami nagyvízi időszakokban lehetőséget biztosítana a felhalmozásra, vagyis a hazai Duna-szakasz vízjárása közvetlenül ki van téve a természetes vízhozam alakulásának. A miniszterelnök azt mondta, folyamatosan egyeztetnek a szlovák és osztrák vízügyi hatóságokkal, és álhírnek nevezte, hogy a két szomszédos ország csökkentené a Magyarország felé érkező dunai vízmennyiséget. By Joseph Epstein Director of the Turan Research Center and Senior Fellow at the Yorktown Institute 0 Share Newsweek is a Trust Project member See more of our trusted coverage when you search. Prefer Newsweek on Google to see more of our trusted coverage when you search. Every country that cannot be a superpower now wants to be called a middle power. Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney built his Davos speech around the term in January, and European officials invoke it at every security conference. South Korea, Australia, Indonesia, Mexico and Turkey organized a grouping around the idea more than a decade ago. Leaders from Riyadh to Astana use it to describe their foreign policies. The label has become so popular that it risks meaning nothing. It should mean something specific: a state strong enough militarily and independent enough economically to bargain with great powers instead of depending on them. By that measure, countries like Poland, South Korea, Taiwan and Azerbaijan qualify. Canada and Western Europe, the loudest new converts, adopted the label after their free ride on American security ended, and they have yet to earn it. For two centuries, from the Congress of Vienna through the Cold War, international politics was studied as the business of great powers. After the political scientist William T.R. Fox coined the word in 1944, it became the business of superpowers. The middle power is the older idea. In 1589, the Italian Jesuit Giovanni Botero sorted states into empires, middle states and small ones. He judged the middle rank the most durable: strong enough to deter predators and modest enough that it never provoked a coalition against itself. Read More on Opinion The term has come back into vogue because the post-Cold War order is fracturing. Rivalry between Washington and Beijing now runs through trade, technology and the Taiwan Strait. Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have shown how quickly distant conflicts can disrupt energy markets and shipping lanes. The major powers increasingly wield tariffs, sanctions and supply chains as weapons. Middle powers respond by hedging. They align with one power on security, trade with another, and build coalitions issue by issue without surrendering their freedom of action. ... Carney told Davos that the world faced "a rupture, not a transition" and that great powers now prey on smaller states. He left out how Canada arrived here. After the Cold War, Ottawa and most Western European capitals took a far larger peace dividend than Washington did. Canada's defense spending fell to about 1 percent of GDP and Germany's to little more. Both governments spent the difference at home, confident that the United States would cover the gap. Their leaders found ample time to criticize American health care, policing and foreign policy, and little time to ask whose navy kept their sea lanes open. Canada met NATO's 2 percent target this year for the first time in decades. Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon's top policy official, called a collective middle-power strategy a "distraction" this summer, and on Canada and Western Europe he has a point. States that cannot defend themselves have little to pool. Canada's talks to buy Swedish surveillance aircraft will not replace reliance on the American defense industrial base. Colby errs in extending that judgment to every state that claims the label. Poland has chosen self-reliance over dependence. It is spending 4.8 percent of GDP on defense this year, among the highest shares in NATO. It is building what it intends to be the largest land army in the European Union. Warsaw buys American Abrams tanks, Patriot batteries and F-35s, along with South Korean K2 tanks, K9 howitzers and FA-50 jets. South Korea turned a war-ravaged economy into a powerhouse in semiconductors, shipbuilding and arms manufacturing. Last year it ranked second in arms sales to NATO's European members, and its shipyards now figure in Washington's plans to rebuild American naval production. Taiwan manufactures the overwhelming majority of the world's most advanced chips. Its government has committed to raising defense spending to 3.3 percent of GDP this year and 5 percent by 2030. Azerbaijan shows how far capability can carry a smaller state. Its army retook the country's occupied territory in 2020 and 2023, and its energy sector supplies Europe. After Russian air defenses downed an Azerbaijan Airlines jet in December 2024, Baku pressed until Putin acknowledged Russian responsibility 10 months later. It has signed strategic partnerships with both Washington and Beijing. On October 3, President Ilham Aliyev told his party congress that China and the United States are the world's two superpowers and "there is no third." Leaving Russia off that list was a striking omission for the leader of a former Soviet republic, and only a state with real independence could afford it. Kazakhstan has built leverage of a different kind. It produces roughly 40 percent of the world's uranium and holds critical minerals Washington wants. It anchors the Middle Corridor, which links China and Europe while bypassing Russia. Its diplomacy has been as disciplined as any in Eurasia. This summer, seated beside Vladimir Putin, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev urged the Russian president to end the war in Ukraine. Last November, he brought Kazakhstan into the Abraham Accords. These states will not carry equal weight. Economic leverage buys Kazakhstan room to maneuver, while the armies of Poland, South Korea and Azerbaijan buy those states a say over outcomes. In the emerging order, the middle powers that combine economic independence with real military strength will call more of the shots. Colby's warning that access to American weapons "is a privilege, not a right" works on Ottawa and far less well on capitals with alternatives. When Turkey could not obtain Patriot batteries on terms it accepted, it bought Russia's S-400. Washington's leverage over strong middle powers depends on offering them something. The United States should spend its diplomatic capital where it returns the most: coproduction with Seoul and Warsaw, arms and trade for Taipei, and corridors and mineral deals for Baku and Astana. Some of these states hedge and some align firmly with Washington, but all of them lean toward the power that treats them as partners. Until Canada and Western Europe build the strength that earns the title, their middle-power status is a slogan. Joseph Epstein is the director of the Turan Research Center.
